name: Lithium
short: An ion with uncertain mechanism; proven in mania and in preventing suicide.
mechanism: An **ion** whose mechanism is uncertain. Candidates are in signal transduction: inhibition of **inositol monophosphatase**, modulation of **G proteins**, and regulation of growth-factor and plasticity genes via cascades including inhibition of **GSK-3** and **protein kinase C**.
uses: **Manic episodes** and prevention of recurrence, especially of mania (perhaps less for depression)
Well established to help **prevent suicide** in mood disorders
Bipolar depression and augmentation in unipolar depression (not approved; lower doses; out of favor)
Added to serotonin/dopamine agents in mania

facts.text: The antimanic agent lithium **may target GSK-3**, one of only three enzymes targeted by psychotropic drugs.

Used for more than 50 years. Modern expert use: one member of a **portfolio**, often **once daily** and at **lower doses** combined with other agents, rather than high-dose monotherapy for euphoric mania.

sideEffects.e: GI upset: dyspepsia, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea
Weight gain, hair loss, acne, tremor, sedation, decreased cognition, incoordination
Toxicity risk: **narrow therapeutic window**; monitor plasma levels

name: Valproate
short: Mania-minded anticonvulsant with uncertain mechanism (VSSC, GABA, signal transduction).
mechanism: Mechanism uncertain. Three hypotheses: altering **VSSC** sensitivity (binding channel or regulatory units, or inhibiting phosphorylating enzymes) to reduce glutamate release; **enhancing GABA** (more release, less reuptake or slower breakdown by GABA-T); and regulating **signal transduction** (inhibiting GSK-3, PKC and MARCKS; activating ERK, BCL2 and GAP43). May also act at calcium channels and indirectly block glutamate.

targets.note: One possible way it enhances GABA

uses: **Acute mania** (proven); commonly long term to prevent mania (less established)
Possibly **rapid cycling** and **mixed** episodes (some experts), usually in combination
Epilepsy; **migraine**

facts.text: The antimanic agent valproate **may** have actions on GSK-3 (marked with a question mark in Figure 2-14).
Raises **lamotrigine** levels, increasing rash risk unless lamotrigine is titrated slowly (p. 352).

sideEffects.e: Bone marrow, liver and pancreatic toxicity; monitor counts and platelets
Amenorrhea, **polycystic ovaries**, hyperandrogenism, obesity, insulin resistance in women

name: Carbamazepine
short: Mania-minded anticonvulsant blocking the VSSC α subunit; CYP3A4 inducer.
mechanism: Thought to bind a site **within the α subunit** of **voltage-sensitive sodium channels** in the open conformation, unlike valproate; may also act at calcium and potassium channels and thereby enhance GABA’s inhibitory actions.
uses: **Acute mania** (first anticonvulsant shown to work; FDA-approved later as a once-daily controlled-release form)
Epilepsy; **neuropathic pain**

sideEffects.e: Profound early **bone marrow suppression**: monitor blood counts

Perhaps the most effective unapproved drug for neuropsychiatric symptoms of dementia, but side effects and **drug interactions** limit it in the elderly.

name: Lamotrigine
nbn: Voltage-sensitive sodium channel blocker; glutamate release inhibitor
short: Depression-minded anticonvulsant that prevents recurrence of both poles; rash risk.
mechanism: Binds the **open-channel VSSC α subunit** (like carbamazepine) and may also act at calcium and potassium channels. Uniquely, it may **reduce glutamate release**, via VSSCs or an unidentified synaptic action, which could explain why it treats and stabilizes **from below**.
uses: Prevention of **recurrence of mania and depression** in bipolar disorder (approved)
**Bipolar depression** (believed effective by experts; not FDA-approved)
Added to serotonin/dopamine agents when depression is not controlled

sideEffects.via: Minimized by very slow titration and managing interactions (e.g., **valproate** raises levels)

facts.text: Table 7-3: epilepsy ++++, treat from above +/−, stabilize from above ++++, treat from below +++, stabilize from below ++++.
Not approved for mania, perhaps because its sodium channel action is too weak or its long **titration** prevents the quick action mania needs.

name: Oxcarbazepine
short: Carbamazepine relative and prodrug; better tolerated but unproven in bipolar disorder.
mechanism: Structurally related to, but not a metabolite of, carbamazepine. A **prodrug** converted to the 10-hydroxy (monohydroxy) derivative **licarbazepine**, whose active S form is **eslicarbazepine**; presumed to bind the open-channel VSSC α subunit.
uses: Epilepsy
Used **off-label**, especially for mania, despite never being proven in acute mania or depression

sideEffects.e: Less sedation, bone marrow toxicity and CYP3A4 interaction than carbamazepine

name: Eslicarbazepine
short: The active S enantiomer of licarbazepine, oxcarbazepine’s active form.
mechanism: The active **S enantiomer of licarbazepine**, through which oxcarbazepine works; presumed VSSC α-subunit binding like carbamazepine.
uses: Anticonvulsant; used off-label, especially for mania

name: Topiramate
short: Anticonvulsant with ambiguous bipolar results; causes weight loss.
mechanism: An anticonvulsant also approved for migraine; Chapter 7 does not detail its mechanism.
uses: Epilepsy; **migraine**
Adjunct to drugs that cause weight gain (**weight loss**)
Tested in stimulant and alcohol use disorders
Bipolar disorder: **ambiguous** trials; not clearly a mood stabilizer

The book says it is combined with **bupropion** for weight loss; the marketed weight-loss combinations pair bupropion with naltrexone and topiramate with phentermine.
Unapproved but may help **alcoholism**; used off-label for **binge eating disorder** with limited efficacy.

name: Riluzole
nbn: Voltage-sensitive sodium channel blocker; glutamate release inhibitor
short: ALS drug that may reduce glutamate release like lamotrigine.
mechanism: Developed to slow **ALS**; theoretically binds **VSSCs** and prevents **glutamate release**, like the action postulated for lamotrigine, to reduce excitotoxicity.
uses: **Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis**
Bipolar depression: theoretical rationale (excess glutamate)
